New transport modes can add to old ones in the same way. If trains are subsidised and the freed airport slots go to longer flights, nothing is replaced. Public money works only if flights are actually capped.

transcript.author: bill-mckibben
transcript.about: I am skeptical. Public money should go first where each euro does most good. Subsidising rail to replace short flights buys emission cuts at a high cost per tonne, and domestic aviation is a small share of emissions. Compare it with cheaper options first: green energy R&D, health, nutrition. Build the rail where the passenger numbers justify the cost.

transcript.author: jason-hickel
transcript.text: Reply to the Ted Nordhaus and Shellenberger comments: abundance through cleaner aviation assumes decoupling will happen fast enough. No evidence shows that it does. Better rail is good, but without a cap on flights it just adds capacity on top. The richest fly most, so limiting their flights is a matter of justice, not gloom.

transcript.author: jason-hickel
transcript.text: Reply to Lomborg: cost per tonne ignores who has already used up the carbon budget. Rich countries are far beyond their fair share, so cheaper options elsewhere do not excuse frequent flying in the North. Public rail also delivers a use value that ordinary people need, which a cost-per-tonne ranking leaves out.

transcript.author: jason-hickel
transcript.about: I endorse it, with a distributional question attached. Short flights are taken mostly by the richer few, while the noise, kerosene emissions and airport land fall on neighbours and on the global South. Public money for rail repays a small part of an ecological debt. The new lines must also not run over villages and farmland without consent.

transcript.author: jason-hickel
transcript.about: Partly endorse. This work never addresses rail directly, so I reason by analogy. Public money for fast electric rail is worth it if the rail offers people better service, especially when nuclear power runs it. Banning or shaming short flights is restraint, and restraint does not scale. Decarbonize through abundance, and fund cleaner aviation as well.

interviews.author: william-nordhaus
interviews.reaction: A carbon price set at the damage each tonne does, applied to flights and trains alike, cuts emissions where cutting is cheapest. Public money for rail is justified only where benefits exceed costs, not as a default replacement for flying.

interviews.author: ivan-illich
interviews.reaction: Replacing short flights with rail is endorsed only if public money pays for slow, frequent, cheap trains and buses open to all. High-speed lines repeat the counterproductivity of speed, which helps a few and makes everyone else more dependent on transport.

interviews.author: bjorn-lomborg
interviews.reaction: Public money should go first where each euro does most good. Subsidising rail to replace short flights cuts a small share of emissions at a high cost per tonne. Rail deserves funding only where passenger numbers and cost-benefit tests justify it, not by default.

interviews.author: ted-nordhaus
interviews.reaction: Public money for fast, cheap, frequent electric rail is a sound climate investment because it gives people a better option instead of asking them to give something up. Rail should win by being better, not because short flights are banned or taxed, and clean aviation deserves funding too.

interviews.author: ramon-fernandez-duran
interviews.reaction: Endorsed. Cheap oil is ending, so short flights will shrink anyway, and the real question is how that decline is shared. Public money should fund everyday regional and conventional rail rather than high-speed showcases, and flights must actually be capped.

interviews.author: andre-gorz
interviews.reaction: Rail should replace short flights with public money, as a shared public provision rather than a carbon price that turns limits into privilege. Faster, cleaner traffic alone changes nothing. Places should be rebuilt so that people need to travel less, under a common norm of enough.

interviews.author: robert-bullard
interviews.reaction: Endorsed on a condition. Rail should replace short flights with public money only if new lines, depots and noise are not pushed onto Black and poor neighbourhoods. Affected communities must consent, and the service must reach people who never fly.

interviews.author: andreas-malm
interviews.reaction: Endorse, and go further: publicly planned rail should replace short flights, and those routes should be banned. Price signals leave the choice to the owners whose profits built the fossil economy. Only planning and state power can retire those assets.

interviews.author: jean-baptiste-fressoz
interviews.reaction: Public money for rail is worth spending, but a takeover is unlikely. Energy history shows new sources add to old ones rather than replace them, so trains will only displace short flights if flights are actually capped. Otherwise mobility simply accumulates.

interviews.author: murray-bookchin
interviews.reaction: Rail should replace short flights, but the shift is a social question before a technical one. Public money spent by national ministries only swaps one hierarchy for another. Federated municipal assemblies should decide routes, fares and land use, and bring work and homes back within human scale.

interviews.author: roger-scruton
interviews.reaction: A qualified endorsement. Public money for rail is justified when it restores local lines and stations that communities love as part of home. It is not justified when it serves national carbon targets, bans imposed from the centre, or campaigns of guilt.

interviews.author: erik-swyngedouw
interviews.reaction: The shift from short flights to public rail deserves support, but only as a political choice. Treated as expert-managed carbon accounting, it depoliticises mobility and leaves growth, property and who decides outside debate.

interviews.author: yayo-herrero
interviews.reaction: Endorsed. Rail funded as a common good puts the sustaining of life ahead of profit. It cuts ecological damage that no ledger counts. It should favour everyday, affordable regional lines that serve the care work daily life depends on, not high-speed showcases.

interviews.author: arne-naess
interviews.reaction: Rail should replace short flights with public money, but only as a shallow first step. The deeper task is to ask why industrial life needs so much fast movement and to seek a life rich in ends and simple in means, rooted in place.

interviews.author: nicole-seymour
interviews.reaction: Publicly funded rail should replace short flights, but as a pleasure rather than a penance. Flight shame and sermons push people away, while cheap, convivial trains win them over. Rail should also serve chosen kin across distance, not a duty to stay put.

interviews.author: bill-devall
interviews.reaction: Rail replacing short flights deserves public money, but it remains reform environmentalism that manages mobility as a resource. The deeper aim is a life simple in means and rich in ends: rooted in place, with less need to travel at all.

interviews.author: jason-hickel
interviews.reaction: Publicly funded rail should replace short flights, but only together with a cap on aviation and absolute cuts in Northern energy use. A modal shift on top of growing demand repeats the green growth illusion. Fair shares of the carbon budget for the South are the goal.

interviews.author: michael-shellenberger
interviews.reaction: Public money for fast, clean, electric rail is justified when it gives travellers something better than flying. Bans, flight shame and managed descent are the politics of limits. Decarbonization comes through abundance and better technology, including cleaner aviation, not through restraint.

interviews.author: terry-anderson
interviews.reaction: Public money that picks a transport mode shields planners from the cost of bad choices. Full prices, clear property rights and a charge for pollution let rail win the routes where it really costs less, without subsidies or bans.

interviews.author: joan-martinez-alier
interviews.reaction: Public rail should replace short flights. Those flights serve a richer minority, while their noise and emissions fall on neighbours and on the South. A carbon price cannot settle this ecological distribution conflict, and new lines must not be forced through poor communities without their consent.

interviews.author: michael-lowy
interviews.reaction: Publicly funded rail should replace short flights as a choice made democratically by need, not by profit. It must be an affordable common service, and short routes should be capped or closed, an emergency brake on aviation growth rather than an addition to it.

interviews.author: bill-mckibben
interviews.reaction: Warming has already changed the planet, so every sector has to cut now, short flights included. Public money should build rail and public transport, and short routes should be capped so the trains replace flights instead of adding to them.

interviews.author: malcom-ferdinand
interviews.reaction: Public rail replacing short flights is endorsed, on one condition: the transition must not leave ashore the island and overseas peoples whose dependence on flying was drawn by colonial routes. A uniform price or a mainland-only plan repeats Noah's Ark.

interviews.author: alain-de-benoist
interviews.reaction: Endorsed, on the grounds of degrowth and rooted localism rather than carbon accounting. Public money should restore regional and branch lines that bind places together. Faster links between metropolises would only extend uniform hypermobility. The deeper aim is less need to travel.

interviews.author: ronald-coase
interviews.reaction: Harm is reciprocal, so making public money or bans the default rule for transport misplaces the question. Each route should be judged by comparing the total costs of the real alternatives, including what state action itself costs and how often it gets things wrong.

interviews.author: jacques-ellul
interviews.reaction: Rail uses less than short flights, but swapping one mode for another keeps the same test of faster, more efficient movement. Publicly funded speed is sold on its benefits and says nothing of its costs. The prior question is why life demands so much travel.
